The Marbled salamander Ambystoma opacum exhibits a life history closely tied to ephemeral wetlands, where females deposit their clutches in dry basins during autumn, waiting for winter rains to flood the nests and trigger hatching. Under controlled laboratory conditions simulating a cool woodland pond, eggs incubated at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] typically require approximately 60 days [ab = approximately 60 days] to hatch, a developmental period that reflects the metabolic constraints imposed by low-temperature embryogenesis. This protracted incubation contrasts sharply with the faster embryonic development observed in some pond-breeding congeners, likely an adaptation to the seasonal unpredictability of autumnal flooding events.

Adult females of this species reach a maximum snout–vent length of 6 cm [Li = 6 cm], a relatively modest size among ambystomatid salamanders that corresponds to an ultimate wet body mass of approximately 1.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 1.3 grams] for reproductively active individuals. The relationship between linear and mass growth in this species follows a standard allometric scaling pattern, and the empirical data indicate that a female approaching this asymptotic mass is fully capable of sustaining a single annual reproductive event. Although the total length including the tail can reach 10.7 cm, the snout–vent measurement provides a more reliable metric for comparing body size across populations and life stages.

Following hatching, the aquatic larvae enter a period of rapid exogenous feeding and growth before undergoing metamorphosis. In individuals reared under a thermal regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the time elapsed since birth at metamorphosis is approximately 60 days , a duration that falls within the broader range of 2 to 9 months reported for wild populations depending on local environmental conditions. This relatively short larval period is characteristic of species that breed in temporary pools, where the risk of pond desiccation places a premium on accelerated development. The transition from gill-breathing larva to terrestrial juvenile involves profound morphological reorganization, including tail resorption and lung development, and is a critical bottleneck in the species' life cycle.

Female Marbled salamanders deposit approximately 100 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 100 eggs per clutch] and produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a reproductive schedule that is paced by the species' energy budget and the seasonal availability of suitable breeding sites. The observed daily reproductive rate is therefore equivalent to 100 eggs divided across the 365 days of the year, and this annual output is sustained only when females have reached a body mass of approximately 25.3 grams, a threshold that ensures adequate yolk provisioning for the developing embryos. At the typical breeding temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the efficiency of vitellogenesis and oviposition is optimized, and the resulting clutch size remains consistently near the species' maximum.

The life cycle of Ambystoma opacum is characterized by a slow pace relative to many other pond-breeding urodeles, with key demographic events spaced across several years. Under a constant temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 1.5 years [tp = approximately 1.5 years], and the maximum recorded lifespan under similar thermal conditions reaches 11.3 years [am = 11.3 years]. These extended juvenile and adult stages reflect a life-history strategy in which delayed maturity and iteroparity compensate for relatively low annual fecundity. The neonatal wet weight at birth is only 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a value consistent with estimates for other Ambystoma species and reflecting the limited yolk reserves available to support early larval growth before the onset of exogenous feeding.
